tracks.title: When FROM reaches past the file
tracks.text: Lesson 09 point 6 — foreign tables. A deep-dive… under the VFS. The parent lesson sold you a sealed disk, and it meant it. Every path bottoms out inside the file… by construction. Nothing the code or the agents do can reach the machine underneath. That is the whole safety story. [curious] It is also, eventually, a wall — because the data you actually care about doesn't live in the file. It lives in Linear… in Asana… in Stripe… in some REST endpoint your team stood up last quarter. This lesson is the seam past that wall. When FROM reaches past the file.

tracks.title: The disk ends at the file's edge
tracks.text: First — the disk ends at the file's edge. And two bad instincts present themselves… both of which undo something. The first instinct — hand the agent the API key and a network socket. [sighs] That demolishes the sealed-disk story the VFS lesson just spent a page building. A steerable agent… with a credential… and an open port… is an exfiltration machine, waiting for the wrong instruction. The second instinct — paste exports into the disk by hand. Honest. Safe. And stale… the moment you save it. So the missing piece isn't a bigger disk… or a looser sandbox. It's a way for FROM to mean past the file when you want it to — without the query engine ever learning what HTTP is, and without the agent ever touching the wire.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A foreign table is an entity name… registered by a data-source plugin… so that FROM, then an entity name, resolves past the file. To a live external source… or a resident local mirror. Instead of to a table inside the workbook's disk. It is the read face of a federation toolkit. And here's the honest scale of it — this is not a new query engine, and not a new primitive. It's a routing decision. An unregistered name falls through to the local VFS, exactly as before. A registered name is handed to a plugin. The whole thing is one regular expression… one fast in-memory map… and a one-callback contract.

tracks.title: One FROM, two destinations
tracks.text: Now the core mechanic — one FROM, two destinations. And it is smaller than you'd guess. Picture the path a query takes. A query walks in — SELECT, something, FROM x. Step one… a single regular expression lifts the entity name off the front of the first FROM clause — just letters, digits, a dash, an underscore. Step two… it asks the registry one yes-or-no question. Is x registered in the source map? Down the yes branch — the matching plugin is called, it goes and gets the data, and the rows come back live, flagged federated true. Down the no branch — nothing exotic happens at all. It returns a plain little atom… not-federated… and the caller quietly does what it always did. It queries the local disk, across every workbook member's store. [curious] And here's the beautiful part. The query engine never learned about HTTP… or GraphQL… or any external protocol. It learned to route on a name. And a plugin learned the rest. One seam… two destinations… and the boundary between them is a single word in the FROM clause.

tracks.title: The whole contract is one callback
tracks.text: The whole contract is one callback — and this is a depth rung, skip it if you like. A data source is one function. The behaviour has exactly one callback — query, taking an entity, a query bundle, and options — returning either ok with a list of rows, or an error. Today that query bundle hands the plugin the raw SQL string, plus its own config. The plugin parses what it needs. The registry lives in fast in-memory storage — rare write, fast read. And four calls reach it. First… register, which binds a name to a plugin module and its config — and after that, the entity is foreign. Second… lookup, which finds the module for a name, or returns nothing — this is what the router calls on every single query to decide the fork. Third… config, which fetches that entity's settings — a URL, a rows path, an env key — and hands them to the plugin. And fourth… entities, which lists the whole foreign namespace. The verdict, in one line — registration is the entire surface. No schema to declare… no migration… no adapter interface beyond that one function. And that deliberate smallness… is exactly why a generic source can make any JSON endpoint a table without writing code at all.

tracks.title: Plugins announce themselves in org
tracks.text: Plugins announce themselves in org. Nobody calls register by hand. Discovery globs the toolkits folder for plugin manifests, and reads a small set of keywords out of each one. The slot — which must say data-source. The entities — a list of names this source owns. The impl — the module that does the work. Plus generic config, like a URL, a rows path, an env key. Now picture the discovery flow as a story with two gates. It globs the manifests… it parses the keywords… and then it checks two things. Gate one — is this slot a data source? Gate two — does the named module actually exist, and export the query function? Pass both gates… and every listed entity registers. [curious] But fail either one — most importantly, if the manifest names a module that doesn't exist yet — and the source is skipped. Silently. Not crashed… not an error. That's a designed kindness. A toolkit can ship its declarative manifest… before its implementation lands… and discovery just treats the gap as not-ready. One honest caveat though — discovery has no automatic call at engine boot. It's invoked on demand. You run discovery… you don't inherit it.

tracks.title: Any JSON API in six lines
tracks.text: Any JSON API… in six lines. The only shipped implementation is also the most useful one — a generic HTTP source that turns any JSON endpoint into a table with zero code. You write a manifest, not a module. Let me read you one a reader could drop in today. Title — orders. Slot — data-source. Entities — shop-order. Impl — the generic HTTP data source. URL — api dot example dot com, slash v1, slash orders. Rows-path — data dot items. And env-keys — SHOP underscore API underscore KEY. That's it. Run discover… and shop-order is now a foreign table. Then query it — SELECT star FROM shop-order — and it comes back federated, with your rows. The rows-path is an optional dotted path that digs into nested JSON — data dot items reaches into the data object, then the items array. Omit it… and the body itself is taken as the array. Now picture the request as a relay where the plugin never opens a socket. The query calls the HTTP source. The source asks the host to make the GET — the comment in the code is exact, the plugin never opens a socket itself. The host fetches it, with a ten-second timeout. A success status returns the body… the source decodes it, digs the rows-path, drops anything that isn't a record, and hands back the rows. [curious] And when it fails… it fails honestly. A 500 comes back as an error, with the status, propagated untouched. No URL at all… is an error too. Clean.

tracks.title: One audited path for the key
tracks.text: One audited path for the key. That manifest named an env key — and the way that key reaches the request is the whole trust story. The plugin never reads the environment directly. It calls one audited function — fetch, with the key name — and the source builds the authorization header itself. Credentials have one home… not a scatter of lookups across plugin code. Now follow the ladder of precedence, step by step. The plugin asks fetch for the key. Step one — fetch tries the deploy's resolver first. That's a function… the keychain or broker seam… and if it returns a value, that value wins. Step two — if the resolver returns nothing, or an empty string, it falls back to the host environment. Step three — and if the key is missing everywhere, fetch returns nothing… and the request still goes. Bare. With no auth header at all. The test pins this exactly — it asserts the literal bearer header when a token is present. [excited] The key never enters plugin code as a string the plugin went and fetched. And the toolkit that ships the manifest… contains no credentials at all.

tracks.title: The second face — a resident mirror
tracks.text: The second face — a resident mirror. Live reads are one face. But for agents… you usually want the other one. Don't let the agent reach out. Run a daemon that pulls the world in — renders the rows as plain org headlines on the disk — and let the agent read the disk, like any other workbook. That daemon's pure core runs SELECT star FROM the entity… renders the rows to org… and writes them into the disk, under a sync folder. And the render is mechanical, so let me read you the exact bytes it writes, given two rows — one with id one and title alpha, one with id two and title beta. At the top, a title line — shop-order, synced. Then a synced-from line, marking where it came from. Then, for the first row… a headline — star, alpha, tagged task. Below it a properties drawer — ID one… TITLE alpha. Then the same for beta — a headline tagged task, and a drawer with ID two, TITLE beta. The title for each headline is picked by a cascade — the first present of title, then name, then summary, then id. Every key goes into the drawer… upper-cased. Any non-scalar value is JSON-encoded. The daemon ticks on a default five-minute interval — and notably… it does not pull at boot. A freshly started daemon has scheduled its first tick… but has not yet reached out. Picture the loop as a one-way conveyor. The timer fires. The daemon runs the query. The rows come back. It renders them to task headlines… and puts them into the disk. And the agent, on the far side… only ever opens that file. It reads org text. It never appears anywhere near the query… the timer… or the source.

tracks.title: Why the mirror is the safe face
tracks.text: Why the mirror is the safe face. That one-way conveyor… is the entire safety argument. And it is structural — not a policy you have to trust. The agent never touches the API… and never sees the credential. The daemon holds the key. The agent holds nothing. Their only contact surface is org headlines on disk. Picture two zones, with exactly one bridge between them. On the left — inside the workbook and its disk — the agent reads, and only reads, the synced task file. On the right — outside — the daemon holds the credential and pulls from the real API. And exactly one edge crosses between them… carrying org headlines… in one direction only. [excited] The agent could be fully steered by a hostile instruction… and there is still nothing on its side of the bridge but text someone else already fetched. And the structure is what makes that hold. The daemon is a supervised process, driven from a daemon node in a sync face — not something an agent inside the workbook spawns or steers. And the direction is one-way by construction. The pure core only ever reads the source… and writes the disk. There is no write-back path in it at all. And the toolkit that wires it all together… holds no creds itself. The credential lives with the host… never the toolkit.

tracks.title: Pick your face
tracks.text: Pick your face — a depth rung, skippable. A federation toolkit gives you two ways to read past the file… and they trade differently. Let me give you the verdict rather than every cell. The live read — FROM the entity directly — is current, fetched per query, and the rows live nowhere, transient. The host holds the key, at query time. And if it fails, the error surfaces right then. The resident mirror is the other one. As fresh as its last tick — five minutes by default. The rows live on disk, in the sync file. The daemon holds the key… never the agent. And the agent's only contact surface is org text. So the rule in one sentence. Reach for the live read when freshness per query matters, and the caller is trusted code that can handle an error inline. Reach for the resident mirror when an agent is the reader — because it moves the credential and the network entirely out of the agent's world… and leaves it nothing but text. The specialized connectors — Linear, Asana, a cursor-based sync — are authored shape, with planned implementations. Same one callback… refined.

tracks.title: What FROM does not do
tracks.text: The honest part — what FROM does not do. Because the trick is easy to oversell. First — no predicate pushdown. The generic HTTP source never reads the SQL. SELECT id FROM x WHERE y equals one… and SELECT star FROM x… do the identical thing. They GET the URL… and return every row. WHERE and projection are applied locally, after the fetch. Second — no cross-source joins. A query goes wholly to a plugin, or wholly to the local disk. The first-FROM-wins regex makes that a hard fork. You cannot join a foreign entity against a local table in one statement. Third — the mirror is a point-in-time full replace. Each pull writes one file, replacing the whole thing. No cursor… no incremental sync, in the generic path. Fourth — discovery is on-demand, not automatic. Registration happens when you run it… not when the engine starts. Fifth — only one implementation ships. The generic HTTP source is real and tested. The Linear, Asana, and task-sync modules do not exist in this repo — and their own manifests say so. They're fixtures, skipped on purpose. And one last collision to defuse. There are CLI verbs… mirror, and federate… but those are about git repository federation. A completely different construct… that happens to share the words. Nothing on this page is that.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Does WHERE filter on the server? Not with the generic source. The plugin gets the raw SQL… but the shipped HTTP source ignores it — it GETs the URL and returns every row. WHERE is applied locally, after the fetch. A specialized connector can translate the SQL into its own API's language. The generic one does not. Can the agent see the API key? No — and not by policy. With the mirror face, the daemon holds the key, and the agent only ever reads org headlines off the disk. The credential is never on the agent's side of the bridge. What if a manifest names a module that doesn't exist? It's skipped… silently… by design. That's what lets a toolkit ship its manifest before its implementation lands. Where does the mirror land? In the workspace volume, by default, under a sync folder — sync, slash, the entity name, dot org. Right where any other workbook file lives. And — is this the federate thing? [chuckles] No. Those CLI verbs are git federation. Sharing the word… nothing else.

tracks.title: Back up to the VFS
tracks.text: So that's foreign tables. Not a new query engine… not a new primitive. A routing decision — one word in the FROM clause that decides whether you stay inside the file… or reach past it. And for agents, the safer face is the one that reaches in your stead — the daemon holds the key, the agent reads only text, and the airgap is made of construction, not policy. [curious] This deep-dive picked up exactly where the VFS lesson's honesty section left off — the disk ended at the file's edge… and this was the seam past it. So the way back up is short. Return to the VFS — lesson nine — for the sealed disk this whole page reaches past. Everything here… was built on that one boundary.
